Important Chemicals in Human Body
• Water
• Most abundant inorganic compound (60%–80% of volume of living cells)
• Important functions:
• (1) Useful solvent
• Dissolves many substances for chemical reactions in body
• Body’s major transport medium
• (2) Stabilize body temperature
• Example: Sweating
• (3) Cushioning to protect organs
• Example: cerebrospinal fluid cushions nervous system organs
• (4) Lubricant to enhance movement
• Example: synovial fluid in joints

quotation_candidates.quotation: Physiology L1: Human Body and Chemicals
• Background: What is physiology?
• Overview of organ systems in human body
• Important chemicals in human body
• Physiology is scientific study of:
• normal conditions and activities of a living organism
• and functions and mechanisms of body parts for maintaining survival.
• Content of “human physiology”:
• (1) Normal conditions of human body
• (2) Functions of human cells, tissues, and organs for achieving normal conditions
• The structures and positions of human body parts are highly related to their functions!
• Thus, learning (3) basic anatomy of each organ is essential for understanding the physiological functions!
• The organization of the human body can be broken down into several levels, from the simplest to the most complex, namely:
• Chemical level: different chemicals (E.g. proteins)
• Tissue level: groups of similar cells
• Organ level: discrete structure, which contains two or more types of tissues, for specific functions
• Organ system level: several organs that work closely together
• Organism level: all organ systems combined to make the whole organism
several organs that work together
• Human body is made of chemicals
• Four types of important chemicals in human body
• Most abundant inorganic compound (60%–80% of volume of living cells)
• Dissolves many substances for chemical reactions in body
• (2) Stabilize body temperature
• (3) Cushioning to protect organs
• Example: cerebrospinal fluid cushions nervous system organs
• (4) Lubricant to enhance movement
• Example: synovial fluid in joints
• Simple sugars and complex carbohydrates
• Molecules are made up of 3 types of atoms - C, H, and O
• (1) Monosaccharides: simple sugars
• (2) Disaccharides: combination of 2 monosaccharides
• (3) Polysaccharides: complex carbohydrates
• Contain 3-7 carbon atoms in each molecules
• General formula: (CH 2 O) n (n: number of carbon atoms)
• Directly used by cells for energy production
• Combination of two monosaccharides by dehydration
• Too large to pass through cell membranes
• Must be broken into monosaccharides before entering cells
• Sucrose (table sugar): Glucose + Fructose
• Lactose (milk sugar): Glucose + Galactose
• Polysaccharides (Complex carbohydrates)
• Formed by combination of many monosaccharides
• Fiber (Cellulose): Polysaccharide that forms cell wall of plant cell
• Starch: carbohydrate storage form used by plants
• Glycogen: carbohydrate storage form used by animals
• All 3 examples are formed by combination of many glucose molecules!
• Human digestive system cannot break down fibers!
Major function in human cell is providing a ready and easily used source of fuel.
Glucose is usually the preferred fuel. When glucose is broken down in cell,
chemical energy is released for other reactions in cell.
Excess glucose molecules are changed to glycogen or fat and stored.
• Contain atoms C, H, O, and sometimes contain atom P
• 3 fatty acids + 1 glycerol molecule
• Energy storage (Triglyceride); Fuel (Fatty acid)
• Insulation: Subcutaneous fat reduce heat loss
• Protection: Fat tissues surrounding organs to absorb shock
• 1 glycerol + 2 fatty acids + 1 phosphate group
• Forming cell membrane of human cell
• Four interlocking ring structures
• Cholesterol, Vitamin D, Steroid hormones, and Bile salts
• Cholesterol is used to make vitamin D, steroid hormones, and bile salts in human body
• Contain atoms C, H, O, N, and sometimes atoms S and P
• Formed by amino acids held together by peptide bonds
Amino acids held together by peptide bonds
• Four structural levels result in different shapes and functions
The 3-dimensional folding shape of a protein molecule is important for its function!
E.g. forming the specific active site of an enzyme!
• Proteins unfold and lose their functional 3-D shape
• General Functions of Proteins:
• Structural framework/ Mechanical support: E.g. Collagens in bones, cartilages, tendons, etc.
• Movement: Contractile proteins in muscle cells
• Enzymes: Regulate rate of chemical reactions in human body
• Body defense: Antibodies released by immune cells are used to defense against foreign substances
• Membrane proteins: forming cell membrane and acting as receptor proteins or transporter proteins
• the largest molecules in the body
